proposal.original_claim_summary: Trump Claims Retroactive Self-Pardon for Crimes Committed as President
proposal.original_synopsis: After returning to power in January 2025, Trump asserted that he had effectively pardoned himself for any crimes committed during his first presidential term, building on his legal team's arguments that presidents have absolute immunity from prosecution for official acts. The claim built upon the Supreme Court's 2024 ruling in Trump v. United States, which granted broad presidential immunity. Legal scholars noted that self-pardoning has never been tested in court, and the DOJ's longstanding position is that sitting presidents cannot be indicted — making self-pardons a legally unprecedented and untested concept. The assertion further cemented Trump's posture that the presidency placed him categorically above criminal law.

proposal.original_claim_summary: Trump Ends All Federal Support for Contraceptive Access
proposal.original_synopsis: In February 2025, the Trump administration eliminated federal programs and funding streams specifically supporting contraceptive access, including grants for contraceptive counseling, over-the-counter contraception access initiatives, and emergency contraception stocking requirements. The administration rescinded the Affordable Care Act contraceptive mandate guidance that had required employer health insurance plans to cover contraception without cost-sharing, enabling a broad exemption for any employer citing moral or religious objections. Public health organizations estimated that millions of women would lose free contraceptive coverage under employer-sponsored health plans. The rollbacks occurred simultaneously with the defunding of Title X and elimination of Planned Parenthood Medicaid participation, creating a compounding elimination of reproductive healthcare access for low-income women.
